doc.title: Rossano Sportiello interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 2, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Harry Allen, Scott Hamilton and the unplanned church duet
summary: Harry Allen and Scott Hamilton also avoid set lists; he describes a 75-minute duet concert with Hamilton in an Italian church with no microphones.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: I can picture if you had become a dancer instead of a piano player, that you would have chaffed at the idea of this choreographer telling you, “move here, then you move there and then you move like this.”

Yeah, yeah. But you know with players like Harry Allen, you know, wonderful tenor player. We go on stage and until the very last minute Harry doesn’t know what he’s going to play. And then he’ll start something and we play it. That sometimes is risky but you know, I remember a few years ago with Scott Hamilton, another wonderful tenor player. I was exchanging this opinion of mine about the freedom of not having a set list. And I wanted to see what was his feeling about it. And he said, “thank goodness that at least there is one more person that thinks this way. I don’t want to be thinking what I’m going to be playing before the concert. I want to just go on stage and then be inspired to

play something. Why do I have to make a set list before?” So one time we had this duet concert in Italy. Just me and Scott. And it was a beautiful church and we had no microphones. Just the piano and the saxophone. And with the perfect acoustics. Not too dry but not too wet. You know what I mean? And so I said, “Scott, let’s do this kind of concert. You start with any song you want. And if I know it I’ll join you. Otherwise you play by yourself. And then I’ll start with a song and of course you’ll know it,” because both Scott and Harry, they know everything. And we played one hour 15 minutes concert. One set. I was one hour 15 minutes of music. From one tune to the other without speaking one word. And the most exciting thing was the audience sensed right away what we were doing and they knew that there was nothing established before, and they were just, you felt like they were being part of that. And they were wondering, now what is he going to do. Now what is he going to — and it was the most beautiful. No one was afraid of making mistakes. Because when you get that kind of freedom, and you put one of the starting point is that — you know there’s nothing wrong if you don’t know a tune, you play by yourself. Now of course we were trying to play tunes that we kind of assumed that we knew. It’s not that you really challenged someone just to play the most obscure stuff. Because that’s — you want to play together.
Yeah. Then it becomes sort of like a competition.
Like, “I’ll bet you don’t know this one.”
Yeah. That doesn’t make sense. I mean you want to play together.
